A condo special assessment needs your own cash calendar, even when the building has a reserve

Four graphics distinguish ordinary strata fees, an owner-level assessment, personal saving and the cash available at each instalment deadline.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Prepare personal cash for an independently confirmed assessment calendar

An independently entered owner-level assessment schedule, not a calculation of legal liability or of a building’s funding adequacy. Equal instalments are due at the start of their selected months, before that month’s personal saving arrives. Ordinary strata fees and all other household bills must already be paid outside this reserve. The strata corporation’s operating and reserve funds are not personal accessible cash and are not deducted from the entered owner assessment. Cash earns zero interest. Every bill can use only personal cash then available; unpaid amounts remain separate, without automatic borrowing or later retrospective payment. New saving continues through the full displayed horizon and is not capped after the final instalment. Provincial rules, voting, unit entitlement, sale adjustments, interest on arrears and actual assessment dates require independent confirmation.

The central idea

A building reserve and a personal reserve do different jobs. Once an owner assessment is independently confirmed, test every payment date against cash that is actually yours to use.

01

Keep the building’s money separate from your personal cash

A condominium or strata corporation may hold funds for common expenses while an owner separately keeps a household reserve. The two balances are not interchangeable. A contribution already made through strata fees does not become personal cash available to pay a new bill.

British Columbia’s official guidance distinguishes special levies from ordinary monthly strata fees and describes the corporation’s contingency reserve fund. Those sources provide context for the separation in these graphics. This article does not calculate legal approval, unit entitlement, who owes an assessment on a sale or whether the building’s reserve is adequate.

The starting point for the tool is an independently confirmed assessment amount allocated to one owner, with a payment calendar. Enter that owner-level amount once. Do not subtract an assumed share of the building reserve again unless the actual assessment calculation has already been formally changed. A building balance is not a personal account you can simply withdraw.

02

An assessment sits beside the monthly fee

The first chart compares an ordinary month with the selected assessment months. The ordinary strata fee continues in both. The extra segment is the assessment instalment. This makes a cash commitment visible without suggesting that the regular fee automatically stops while an assessment is being paid.

The original example assumes an owner-level assessment of CAD 18,000, paid in three equal CAD 6,000 instalments at the starts of months six, nine and twelve. The ordinary monthly strata fee is CAD 500 and is already funded outside the personal assessment reserve.

The displayed month types are not an annual total. There can be many ordinary months between instalments. Before using the reserve contribution field, confirm that mortgage or rent, strata fees, taxes, insurance and ordinary living costs are already in the main household budget. The tool assumes the remaining monthly saving is available after those commitments.

03

Check the reserve before the bill, rather than after the next deposit

The second chart follows the personal assessment reserve. Each instalment comes at the start of its month. That month’s new saving arrives at month-end. A transfer received after a bill cannot make the earlier payment timely.

With CAD 5,000 already earmarked and CAD 400 saved monthly, the original example funds the first CAD 6,000 instalment. It does not fund all of the next two. The separate deadline bars retain total unfunded assessment bills of CAD 8,600, even though continued deposits leave CAD 5,200 in the reserve at month twenty-four.

This is a useful distinction between a balance and a successful funding calendar. The positive ending account is not proof that the payments were affordable when due. Unpaid bills are neither forgiven nor paid from automatic credit. Later deposits remain available for later uses; they do not silently cure the earlier shortfalls.

04

The last deadline is not always the binding one

The fourth chart calculates the monthly contribution needed to fund every deadline. For an instalment due in month m, only m − 1 month-end deposits have arrived. The test compares cumulative bills due by that month with opening reserve plus those earlier deposits.

For each deadline after month one, the required monthly saving is (cumulative assessment due − opening reserve) ÷ deposits received before the deadline, floored at zero. The tool takes the greatest requirement across all instalments. With the original schedule, that is approximately CAD 1,181.82 monthly. Rounding a real standing transfer down could leave a small shortfall.

A month-one instalment needs opening cash. If it exceeds the opening reserve, no amount saved later each month can fund it on time. The matrix marks that case unavailable instead of dividing by zero or pretending the first transfer arrived early. Different approved instalment dates would require a new calendar, not a more optimistic label.

05

Use the cash result alongside the actual assessment documents

The tool assumes equal instalments at a regular spacing. An actual resolution may have unequal amounts, different dates, conditions or interest consequences. Use its confirmed schedule when preparing an implemented plan, and verify the applicable provincial rules and responsibility before a purchase or sale.

If the model shows a gap, distinguish possible sources of funding: personal cash already accessible, new affordable saving before the bill, a separately confirmed funding arrangement, or a formally changed payment schedule. None is supplied automatically here. Selling an investment or borrowing also creates its own timing, cost and tax questions.

  1. Confirm the amount allocated to the owner and every due date.
  2. Keep corporate reserves and personal reserves on separate ledgers.
  3. Fund ordinary strata fees in the main budget.
  4. Check cash before each assessment instalment.
  5. Retain every unfunded bill until a workable solution is identified.

The objective is a realistic personal funding calendar. It is not a prediction of a future levy or a recommendation that a particular building should collect or spend its reserves.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Province of British Columbia · Special levies in stratas ↗

    Official BC guidance reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports distinguishing a specific-purpose special levy from ordinary monthly strata fees. BC procedures are jurisdiction-specific. This calculator does not determine approval, allocation, responsibility on a sale or the legality of an assessment.

  2. Province of British Columbia · The contingency reserve fund ↗

    Official BC guidance reviewed 25 October 2026. Describes a strata corporation’s fund and contributions, which are not a personal savings account refundable to an individual owner. The hypothetical owner assessment and personal reserve below are entered independently.
